titleStmt.title: Paraphrase of Dionysius's Ixeutica; or, On Bird-catching

sourceDesc.p:
Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un helleniste) a partir du texte grec du corpus zoomathia sous zoo47/1g_1 (traite d'ornithologie et de chasse aux oiseaux, paraphrase en prose par Eutecnius, transmise sous le nom de Denys [Ps.-Denys], d'apres le poeme perdu de Dionysius, Ixeutika). Le texte grec source est issu du Thesaurus Linguae Graecae (TLG, University of California, Irvine). La structure du texte source (edition > textpart livre [3, n=1-3] > textpart chapitre [77 au total] > paragraphe continu) est integralement preservee ci-dessous, div par div. Seul zoo47/1g_1.xml (la paraphrase en prose continue) a ete traduit ; zoo47/1g_2.xml (transcription brute vers-a-vers du TLG, fragmentee en 967 balises

tres courtes melant texte, numeros de vers et marqueurs d'apparat) n'a pas ete retenu pour cette traduction, la reconstruction d'une prose suivie a partir de cette source fragmentaire presentant un risque d'erreur trop eleve sans reference philologique supplementaire. Ouvrage zoologique a part entiere : description des moeurs de 77 especes d'oiseaux (livres I-II) puis techniques de chasse aux oiseaux par espece (livre III). Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un helleniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte grec deja present dans le corpus sous zoo47/1g.

div.p: Since God, in his goodness, has given you, who hold the rudder of all the earth and sea, both wisdom and love of learning, and since you wish to add to the many things you already know everything that the poet Dionysius has written concerning winged creatures, come, let us fulfill this service for you too, so that you may know the birds — both those that, from love of a moist diet, delight in rivers or lakes or even the sea, and those that fly over mountains or plains — and may be able to name each one, thoroughly understanding their habits, their skills, their strength, their desires, and the ways of hunting them. It is a pleasant and not graceless sight to see a swift bird caught in the bonds of a snare, or perched on the branch of a tree, on a reed which some hunter has smeared with birdlime and holds upright, so that the bird sticks fast and is pulled down; or one that has come to rest for a while on some bushes, and become entangled in the many-holed folds of the nets, so that this rest becomes its final and fatal one. And this too is a clever and charming practice: when the winter season has already come on, men cover a tree with branches and leaves not its own, and, having set among the branches certain rods smeared with birdlime, they set it up in the fields, hanging cages from it; in these are birds that are indispensable to the hunters for the catching, for by their songs they persuade the rest to draw near and settle on these false branches; and, as soon as they alight there, they are caught at once. And indeed one may see very many birds caught in snares too, which men are accustomed to set by placing some food beneath the bushes; and they are caught in other ways as well, each of which you shall learn, if you will listen kindly, in order. Very many kinds of winged creature, then, fly through the moist air.

Of all birds, one must give first place to the eagles, since nothing certain can be said about griffins, which they say are reared in the marshes of the wealthy Arimaspians, and dig gold out of the earth; and they say these Arimaspians have not two eyes each, but one.

We know the kind and the strength of eagles, and how far they surpass the rest of the birds, so that they are believed to perch even near the thunderbolts, by the very scepter of Zeus. They fly easily above the air and up to the very aether, and they see sharply all the way down to the earth — or perhaps even through it — so that not even the smallest little creatures escape their notice when they are in need of food, even if they should be covered by bushes. They delight in the flesh of lambs, and fawns, and the swiftest hares, and would not eat a dead thing, unless some animal had been killed and taken by themselves. As a remedy for sickness they eat tortoises, and, as for drink, the blood of the animals they hunt suffices them, so that they would not drink water. They inhabit the peaks in the mountains, conspicuous and high, whether they need rest after the hunt, or wish to build nests for their young, so that they seldom come down to the plains from the rocks, but for the most part look upon the sky itself close at hand. And when it is time to give birth, they bring a certain stone and place it in the hollow of their nests, so that they may give birth in due season, and so that what is born may not be pushed out, unfinished, before its time, by the mother's own strength. There is, however, nothing certain to be known about this stone: some say it is brought from the Caucasus mountains, others from the shore of the Ocean, and that it is exceedingly white, and full within of a kind of breath, so that it even produces a sound, if it is shaken. If a woman in labor should have it bound to her, it will prevent the infant from slipping. And if it touches boiling water in a cauldron, it will altogether overcome the power of the fire. Eagles also care very greatly for the legitimacy of their offspring, and they judge their young by flying them against the rising sun; and whichever is overcome by the light, or closes its eyes, is not thought legitimate, but a bastard, and is driven from the nest, and the pity of the other birds supplies it with food, just as neighbors are accustomed to feed orphaned children with their own surplus, relieving both the compulsion and the need of their poverty; yet such nourishment never brought the young eagles to the strength of their fathers.

As for the ospreys, it is not even possible for men to see them continually; for they inhabit the roughest rocks, and build their nests for their young on the highest ravines, perching on the cliffs in place of tree-trunks or branches. They love their young extraordinarily, and if some rustic should secretly steal a young osprey unnoticed, the mother will disdain food, mourning, but will not fly far from the nest; she will fill everything with her laments, and one might say she mourns like a woman, and floods her cheeks with a stream of tears. Their cheeks and their chin are full of feathers, so as to display something like a beard down to the neck; and this is a distinctive mark peculiar to ospreys. They are the only birds that feed on stones, and on the bones of long-dead animals — if they can swallow them, gladly passing down whatever comes their way at once, but the larger ones they seize with their talons and, flying up, drop them onto the rocks again and again, so that, once shattered, they may eat them. Black ivy, if eaten, prevents them from falling ill.

Vultures mate by mounting one another, but in vain, and could never beget young by coupling in this way; rather, whenever they are disposed toward laying eggs, like the tigers among wild beasts, they turn their hindquarters toward the west wind, and are made pregnant by its breath; and they say that from this comes their swift perception of scent, even if some animal should die far away. They are insatiable for food beyond all other birds, so much so that they even war with one another over it, and the one stronger in strength drives off the rest, holding out one wing as a shield, and with the other driving away his fellows; but if this one, once sated, withdraws, the rest fall upon the food together, until one of them again drives off the weaker ones. No one could easily find the nests of vultures, for they are in places most impossible to reach. Delighting greatly in the stench of the dead, they hold perfumes in such abhorrence that they would not even touch a dead animal, if someone had anointed its flesh with perfume.

There are several kinds of hawks: some are swift for hunting, especially deadly to doves and wood-pigeons; others catch the smaller birds; others yet are most sluggish and reluctant to fly, so that they wish to be fed by others, and set out for the hunt late in the day, and attack only frogs. Others still share the hunt with men, being kept on leashes and frightening the birds that are hunted; these are enemies to larks and swallows, and in this respect one might call them kin to Tereus. And they suffer from weak eyesight more than any other kind of bird, so that they even know the cure for this affliction: it is the sap of wild lettuce, which it is the custom to squeeze out for hawks, as a remedy.

One could call nothing more shameless than kites; for they often swoop even upon men's very hands, and destroy the chicks of domestic fowl, and cause the greatest distress especially to women. They pay, however, a fitting penalty: at a certain fixed time of year they suffer most wretchedly in their feet. It is also said that they never perch on the pomegranate tree, nor wish even to look at it. And there is a story about them, incredible though it is, which nonetheless prevails: that a man who had lost his wife, and had a daughter by her named Side, looked upon the girl shamefully, so that she, to avoid her father's embrace, killed herself upon her mother's tomb; then, they say, the gods, taking pity on her suffering, made the earth send up the pomegranate tree from her blood; but the father, turned into a kite, flees far off the reminders of his misfortune, and refuses to perch upon that tree.

The birds called memnons are a race of the blackest Ethiopians; they abandon Ethiopia, since it is unsuited to their breeding, because of its excessive heat, and they are unwilling even to build nests there, since the sun would surely scorch their eggs at once; they set out toward the north and Thrace; and, arriving at the Hellespont and Troy, they fight one another over the tomb of Memnon, and one might compare the sound of their wings to the clashing of shields. Then, ceasing their battle, they wash themselves in the stream of the Aesepus, and roll in the dust on the sand, turning about, and, settling on the tomb of Memnon, dry their wings in the rays of the sun, and scatter the dust that is on them over Memnon's tomb, showing thereby, I think, that, though changed from men into birds, they neglect neither royal honor nor the practice of war.

Concerning crows, we ought to know this: that alone among all birds they do not provide their young with drink, since the throat bursts open at once, immediately after mating. Some say this is the punishment for an ancient fault: for the Crow, ordered to bring water when Coronis was giving birth to Asclepius at Tricca, neglected the order and dallied in lust; and because of this, the wrath of Apollo turns him into a black bird, and makes his throat grow swollen without any drink, which becomes, from then on, most painful for his chicks. And this too is a strange fact about crows: they do not mate until one of them has, as it were, sung a wedding song to the females; and, persuaded by this, they then couple.
With crows, unlike all the other winged creatures, the chicks do not break through the egg forward toward the beak, but backward, and come out putting forward their legs first.

Partridges are extraordinarily fond of stags: they wish to graze together with them, and never wish to leave their side; they accompany them, and run alongside, and, perching on their backs, comb out their hair — so much so that they are readily caught approaching, if a hunter shows them the image of a stag. They contend with one another over mating, and spring incites them to couple; grazing in flocks in the woods, if a female appears, they separate and fight one another, and the female becomes the prize of the victor; and he cries out and rejoices, like a champion who has won gold, or a girl, or some other prize from war. But they do not even allow the females to warm the eggs, and steal them away in their haste to mate; and indeed the females too, being wanton, often neglect the raising of their young. And the species is cunning, so that even the chicks know how a man approaching them must be deceived, covering themselves with leaves, or clods of earth, or whatever else comes to hand — just as octopuses do to fishermen, making themselves resemble whatever rocks they cling to.

Even more than partridges love stags, siskins hate donkeys; and if chicks are being raised in a nest of siskins on some plant, a donkey that comes near the tree kills them all without fail, and, braying, causes a pregnant siskin to miscarry.

The cuckoo, the first to announce spring to the rest of the birds, builds no nest of its own, but eats up the eggs of other birds, and, having laid its own egg in another's nest, withdraws; and another bird, unaware, warms what has been born, until it sees the young birds emerging, but, once it perceives the deceit, abandons them and makes another nest; and the cuckoo then comes and gives food to its own chicks.

To woodpeckers a strange gift has been given by the gods: if anyone blocks up their nest with stones or wood, they take up a certain herb known to them for this purpose, and, bringing it to the mouth of the nest, open it and dislodge all the wedges. And whoever knows that herb will easily undo the locks of doors too.

Shepherds hate titmice, because, when they see goats that have just given birth, they take extraordinary delight in their udders, and, approaching, draw out their milk like kids, and so harm the goats' future capacity to give birth.

Owls, though they do the same thing to sheep, cause no harm at all. But this ought to be known about them: that, wishing to keep ants away from their own chicks, they keep a bat's heart in the nest, since ants are known to leave even their own burrows, if someone places a bat's heart near them.
A certain bird is named 'ikteros' [jaundice-bird] from its color; if a man afflicted with that disease looks upon it, he will at once be rid of the whole sickness.

As for the jay's gifts in mimicking voices, how could one describe them, and how many creatures might it seem to be, as it utters its cries? I once thought, hearing a jay, that I heard a kid bleating, and went looking around the tree, as though it were separated from its mother, on which a jay was perched, crying out; then at once came a lowing, and I thought it was a calf; then it bleated like a sheep, and finally imitated the shepherd's whistle, by which, after grazing, he leads the sheep to drink — so that, when at last I saw it leaping about on the branches, I marveled how great, even among the birds, are the gifts of the gods.
As for parrots, which must be kept not in wooden cages, but in iron ones, nature has led their powers of mimicry as far as even our own human speech.

To nightingales too she has given a wonderful harmony of song; they raise their chicks by song rather than by food alone, reckoning those that sing well to be legitimate, and worthy of every care, but killing those that are silent, as an offspring unworthy of the Attic nightingales — a practice which instills in them such a love of freedom that, if they are caught, they refuse to sing, and cut out their own tongue at once.

Swallows are most familiar with, and share the roof of, men; they were changed into birds when the Thracian Tereus was still a man; but when they saw that he too had been changed into a bird, they fled from the wild places and came to dwell among the houses of men. Yet they do not love the breath of the north wind, nor of the other winds that come from Thrace, and they build their nests turned away from such winds. They feed their chicks in such careful order that, if one who has taken food should move to another spot, they would not give it food again until it returned to its place. And if anyone should blind their young, they cut up the swallow-wort plant with their beak and apply the juice from it to the eyes, and so ward off the harm of the blindness.

The seleukis is a most voracious bird, and arrives among farmers amid the greatest prayers, whenever a multitude of locusts devours the crops; for, eating some, and destroying others merely by their shadow, they easily and quickly excrete whatever they have eaten, and one might say they have come as a foreign ally to men under siege. But if anyone deprives these birds of their due gratitude, they destroy the crop that was saved; and if some madman kills a seleukis, then, when the locusts are shearing the crops, allies of this kind will no longer come to that land.

The wrynecks, dear to sorceress-women, obtain their food in this way: stretching out their long tongues like fishermen a fishing-line, and thrusting it into some path of ants, they receive precisely those hurrying toward it as food, then, drawing the tongue back little by little, eat those they have caught. They constantly move their necks, just as the effeminate men who take the women's part are accustomed to revel in the rites of Rhea.
Turtledoves are the most chaste of all birds, and are content with one marriage; and when the mate has died, the survivor would never couple with another.

For doves, one marriage suffices too; yet they will couple with another, if the first has died, and they make the kiss the beginning of intercourse; the older female would not allow mating before the meeting of the beaks, but the young ones often rush into mating even without kisses. And if there are no females present, contrary to the common law of birds, the males mount one another, and lay eggs — of no use at all for the begetting of chicks.

We also know that domestic hens, without any cocks, and warmed in the hands of women, lay eggs; and for them, if they are in labor, it is useful for easy delivery to pick up a straw from the ground with the beak and place it on their back. Of all winged creatures, we know that cocks delight most in fighting and in mating. They delight especially in light, and announce the day beforehand, as though favored by the sun, and they soothe the labor-pains of their hens by sharing in their pains, so as to sing something gentle and soft to comfort them.

Before all the other birds, while it is still winter, the blackbird lays its eggs, and delights in myrtles, and laurels, and groves of cypress, and flourishing white poplars, and pines, and plane-trees, and double-needled pine-trees, and ivy. There are two kinds of blackbird: some are entirely black, while others have beaks resembling wax, and these are better suited than the others for singing.

The peacock has marveled at its own beauty, and, if someone calls it beautiful, it at once raises itself and displays the flowers of its feathers, mixed with gold, as though showing a meadow, turning them about in a circle with its eyes arranged in order; and these shine along its tail like stars upon it. And if someone, on seeing it, praises its beauty, it will at once vie in glory through its own voice too; but if someone mocks it, it will hide its tail, hating him as a lover of insult. This bird was the guard of Io, when Hera was enraged against her; Hermes killed him, and, once he died, the earth sent up a bird bearing on it the markings of his former eyes.

There is also a bird called the purple-coot from its color; its beak is red, and on its head it has something like a cap, of the kind the Persian archers wear; it is equal in size to domestic fowl, except that it uses longer legs. This bird would never mate in the presence, or under the gaze, of a man; it is by nature chaste, and if some jealous rival should appear, it is distressed, so that it does not even wish to see a man coming together with its own mate; and if it should perceive adultery, it becomes so despondent that it dies of it.

Quails, when they leave their former pastures, fly up together, and cross the sea in a single flight, being the sharpest-sighted of birds, and yet so fearful that they shudder at the sight of the open sea, and close their eyes, and are often caught in the sails of ships, and are hunted by sailors in this manner. And so that they may know whether they have crossed the sea or not yet, they have devised this method of testing: each carries three small stones in its beak, and lets go of them one by one, listening to hear whether it has fallen into water, in which case a longer flight is still needed, or has landed on the earth, in which case the time for rest has come.

Many kinds of birds migrate, so that the measure of their journeys and their travels is known, except only for the storks, about whom no one could say with certainty where they come from, or where they return to again; for some say they come from Lycia, others that they come from Ethiopia, from where the vast water of the Nile spreads out and makes the crops in Egypt fruitful. They are marvelous and quick-witted, whether in guarding against harm, or in repaying a kindness done to them. Indeed I have heard the following story about them: someone broke a stork's leg with a stone; it fell sideways from its own nest, and some women, seeing it weak and limping, took it up and healed it; and, once the affliction was overcome, walking again, it flew off with the rest, and, when spring came round again, it hurried back to the same house — so that it was recognized by the marks of its lameness, and the women rejoiced that it had come to them gladly. Bending down with its long beak, it vomited up before the women's feet a most beautiful precious stone; and they realized that storks are often more eager than men themselves to repay a kindness. In Italy, too, something of this sort is said to have happened: a snake, crawling up from the ground, kept devouring the chicks of certain storks, and again, in the following year, destroyed the second brood of the same birds. So they set out for a foreign land, and, coming back a third time, brought back with them a strange bird, never seen before, shorter than themselves, but with a beak sharp and very large, projecting from its head like a sword. How, I wonder, did they announce to it the misfortune of their own chicks, and by what promises or words did they persuade it to come to their aid? Unless indeed someone should say that birds and beasts speak to one another in ways unknown to us. Now this bird, while the storks had no young as yet, went to the same pastures as those who had summoned it; but once they had nested, it was necessary for some to fly far off and bring food for both the chicks and the guard, while one remained at the nest to watch for the coming snake. And a little later, the snake, coming from its lair, began to scatter the chicks, whose ally stood by them, and struck the snake with its beak; but the snake did not yield, but, rearing up its coiled body and bracing itself upon its tail, drew itself up against it and, struck again, then, arraying itself, hastened to wrap its coils around the bird, using its many coils in vain; for the bird easily evaded it, lightened by its wings; and while the one hastened to kill the chicks, the other hastened to save them, until the snake, worn out by the multitude of its wounds, was destroyed — yet, biting the bird in the struggle, and pouring the venom of its teeth into it, caused all its feathers to fall out. When the time came to return, all the other storks flew off; but those who were mindful of repaying the one who had saved their chicks stayed with the chicks themselves, until new feathers grew round the bird, and it was able to depart together with them.

I have heard that, among the Indians, there is a bird without parents, coming into being apart from any mating, called the phoenix, and they say it lives for a very long time, and in complete fearlessness, so that neither arrows, nor stones, nor reeds, nor snares, however much men attempt to use them against it, can do anything to it. Death, for it, makes the beginning of life: for whenever, grown old, it sees itself grown too sluggish for flight, or the rays of its eyes diminished, it gathers twigs upon a high rock and builds a kind of pyre for its death, or nest for its life; and, as the phoenix sits in the middle of it, the heat of the sun's rays sets it ablaze; and, once it is thus destroyed, a new phoenix is born again from the ashes, and takes up its father's ways, so that this bird comes into being by the light of the sun alone, without father or mother.

We must also speak of the amphibious birds, all those that delight in the sea and settle on the shores and build their nests near the beaches, of which there are many and varied kinds; for the sea nourishes no fewer birds than the land. Yet these do not share a single nature with the land birds: the latter have thinner feathers set upon their flesh, useful for swift flight; but the amphibious birds are covered with feathers that are dense, and altogether unable to be wetted, so that they can swim without being soaked. They also have broad passages in their mouths, through which they easily pass the fish they have caught down to their belly. And most of them have webbed feet, which they use like oars while swimming on the water.

This nature is common to them all, but in power the sea-eagles surpass all the rest, being like the land eagles in appearance, but feeding on fish from the sea, and hunting especially those fish that seem to swim on the very surface of the water, so that even part of their body is visible. Yet the outcome of their hunt is not always favorable: often, setting the curved edges of their talons into fish too large, they cannot lift them, being heavy, into the air, and, dragged down themselves, are destroyed sooner than they destroy their prey, the pain driving the fish toward the bottom of the sea, while for the eagles that lack the strength, it happens that, once they are pierced through, their talons are finally released. These, they say, are the bastard offspring of land eagles, and are for this reason driven out of their fathers' nests, and, being then raised by other birds, come to avoid living on land and to delight greatly in the open sea. Fishermen greet them as a welcome and favorable sight.

There is another bird, small like the lesser gulls, but strong, white in color, and resembling the hawks that kill wood-pigeons, called the plunger: for, watching certain fish as they swim — it can see even down to the depths of the sea — it lifts itself up high, and, drawing in all its feathers, hurls itself into the sea as though falling, cutting through the air more swiftly, one might say, than any arrow, and plunges down as much as a fathom or more; sometimes, having seized the fish, it draws it up and, still flying, devours it while it still writhes. It settles on crags and shores and the reefs that rise a little above the sea, and, for drink, unlike the other birds, it uses not rivers or springs, but seawater; and it spreads seaweed on the rocks beneath its eggs, neither warming them itself nor leaving them exposed to the winds throughout. And these plungers do something remarkable with their eggs: the males take up those that will be male, and the females likewise those that will be female, and, gripping them tight with their feet, fly up into the air and let themselves fall toward the sea, then, following after them into the water, snatch them up again more quickly than the sea can, doing this continually over several days; and so the motion, warming the eggs, brings forth the chicks. And these, as soon as they see the light, cannot bear to linger in the nests, but strive eagerly to follow the flight of their parents; then the parents catch them up and let them fall again into the depths, and again snatch them up hastily, lightening the labor for them; for so they are more quickly taught the manner of their fathers' hunting, and one might compare them to children following their aged father at farming, of whom the father, setting the plow to the oxen, turns over the earth, while the child goes before, scattering grain for sowing, and the father stands over them as they work, teaching and rejoicing at once. The plungers, while still young, catch only small fish, and do not even dare to fly far from the shore, but, grown larger, arm themselves for bigger prey. And of all amphibious birds they die the worst death: for, their sight dulled by old age, they lead themselves out toward the open sea, longing for their accustomed hunt, but, dashed against rocks and cliffs, are destroyed.

The sandpipers too are among the amphibious birds, and run along the shores so often that their running is swifter than their flight — indeed they take their very name from this. They do not attempt large fish, but are content to hunt a little crab, or catch whatever else the waves cast up onto the shores. The males graze together with one another, and the females apart again, and when spring comes on, the females, eager for mating, are the first to approach the males, and sing a little to them, as it were, chirping; and so they call them to mating, and the males, reluctantly yielding to their urging, mate, until they think they have made five eggs through the mating, and each then goes off again to its own pasture, the males taking not the slightest thought any longer for the raising of the young, nor any memory of the mating, while the females toil over the chicks and share the labor between themselves; for some remain in the nests, warming the eggs, while others gather food for those doing the warming, and they do this in turn, warming the eggs by the touch of their feathers; then they lead the chicks, once grown, to the shore, where the males like to graze, and, thus divided, the young follow both the males and the females, so that they resemble sheep separated by shepherds after their mingling at pasture.

Gulls are most beloved by men, and dwell near them as the most familiar of birds; and if they see fishermen drawing in a net, they come near the boats as partners in the catch and, crying out around the nets, demand a share of the catch, and the fishers grant it, throwing some of the fish into the sea; and the gulls run to eat those thrown to them, and, if any other fish escape the nets, receive these too, very readily; so that there is an opinion that they were once men, and the first to discover sea-fishing, and, changed by the will of the gods into birds, still remember their old craft, flying not far from cities and harbors. There are several kinds of gulls: some of them are white, and small like doves; others are larger and stronger than these, and covered with very dense feathers, and some are even larger still than these. Their feathers too are white, except that they are black at the very tips of the wings and around the neck. And all the other gulls grant these their pasture and their perch, and yield to them as to kings; and, as they grow old, their feathers become dark blue, and they nest on the rocks where fresh water most flows down from the land, so that their young use seawater for food, but fresh water for drink, until they are grown strong enough to fly from the nests; then indeed they will use both food and drink from the sea. For speed of swimming, no other bird could rival the gull.

Shearwaters always crave the greatest quantity of food, and could never be satisfied even when starving, and they excrete the fish they eat straight through, so that sometimes they even pass them out still living. And they alone among amphibious birds hunt, fly, and eat all at the same time, feeding especially on conger eels and morays and the other fish that have a slippery body. They also remain submerged underwater for a very long time, and pursue fish like dolphins or dogfish. They are found not only on the open sea, but also on lakes, especially if some disturbance from the winds troubles the sea; for then they do not wish to linger there. And they say that these alone, of all winged creatures, neither utter a sound nor are able to hear.

Pelicans too, which have the longest necks, have no less a desire for food, but do not plunge their whole body under, as shearwaters do; rather, like tumblers, they continually let down their necks, which are a fathom in length, showing their backs above the sea, and devour every fish they meet, taking them in with a huge gaping mouth. And they have a kind of pouch hanging before their breast, into which, in their haste, they cast all their food, sparing neither scallops nor hard-shelled mussels, sending on whatever comes their way together with its shell for the time being; then, once everything is dead, they belch it all up again, and so eat the flesh, but throw the shells far away; for, closed while alive, the shell opens and gapes after death.

One could not call any birds sweeter in voice than the halcyons, nor more beloved by the sea-gods, who grant them a calm, stilling the waves, and complete windlessness at the appointed time of their labor, for seven days in succession, during which they lay and raise their chicks. This is believed to be a gift of the Nereids for love of husband, since Alcyone, once mourning without restraint her husband Ceyx, destroyed at sea, was changed into a bird, but has not forgotten her suffering. They love the sea so much that they set their nests right by the waves themselves, wetting their breast, while resting their tail on the dry land. Nor, like the other birds, do they use twigs from the land, but gather seaweed, and sprigs of vine, and tendrils, and sea-ears, and other plants from the sea, to build their nests. And if it should happen that the male dies, they abstain from food and all drink, and mourn for a long time, and even die of it; and if they are about to cease their song, they say 'Ceyx' repeatedly, and fall silent. But may neither I nor anyone else ever hear the voice of a ceyx-bird; for it signals cares, and deaths, and misfortunes; on which account Zeus has made them graze by night, and pass their time in the most desolate parts of lakes and rivers, so that they do not trouble men.

Herons are most dear to men, and foretell fair weather and storms, turning especially toward that quarter from which the fiercest wind is about to blow, laying their heads down upon their breasts. A sailor, at any rate, would never willingly kill a heron, since fishermen believe that these birds signal to them at sea just as hawks signal to hunters on land. They say too that, when all birds still had a single kind of food, herons were the first to discover prey from the waters, and taught all the rest from their own example; but, growing boastful over this skill, and even claiming that Poseidon himself could not rival them at swimming, they were stripped of their knowledge by the anger of the god — just as they say the Muses did to Thamyras, who boasted greatly of his own singing. From then on, then, all the other birds dive into the water to hunt fish, but herons, deprived of the power to swim, hunt standing on the shore, contriving something clever and charming to deceive the fish: they stand facing away from the sun's rays, so that the fish, not seeing their shadow, do not swerve away. There are countless kinds of them: some are small and white, others varied in color and larger, others yet of middling size; some have no crest on their head, while others have something like a lock of hair hanging down. All of them, while living from the sea, build their nests on the land.
Stilts have thin legs, and take their name from this. A strange thing about them is that, while keeping the lower jaw fixed, they move only the upper one.

Fishermen name another bird the 'kepphos' from its lightness; for it runs over the very surface of the water on its feet, and signals good fortune to fishermen. They stay wherever the finest shoals of fish may be, and follow tunny especially, since these fish, biting the smaller fish into pieces with their teeth, leave behind in the water certain scraps of flesh, on which the kepphoi feed. Indeed they also follow dolphins, making food of the blood of the fish the dolphins have killed. They even eat the very foam of the sea, and one could hardly ever see kepphoi idle or asleep, either on land or at sea, but always either hunting or flying. And they fear thunder so much that, if they hear it, they fall from the air into the sea, whether they are born from the sea itself or from the air; for the earth too sends up certain fruits of its own accord at the sound of thunder.

The 'elaphis' is a bird whose feathers, all over its back, resemble a stag's hairs, and it feeds like the land-dwelling wrynecks, letting down its very long tongue, like a fishing-line, into the water for a long time, and so drawing up, little by little, toward its throat, the fish that has been deceived and has touched it. It was from watching this bird, it seems to me, that fishermen first thought of hanging horsehair from their long reeds.

Divers always love to swim, and would never come to land, whether for the sake of sleep or of food, nor does storm or night compel them to do so, but they remain upon the waves, not fearing the cold, and swim against the wind, so that they are never forced by its violence to be carried onto land against their will.
The same thing is done by the birds called thraikes and by the dytinoi, who come out onto land only, as being safer, when they are about to lay their eggs.

The kirris pays a fitting penalty for her impieties: for, having fallen in love with Minos, and having cut off her father's purple lock, she chose to betray her homeland to Minos; but he, reproaching the betrayal even after his victory, bound her to his ship and let her be dragged through the sea. And so she was changed into a bird, but is hated by all birds, and if a sea-eagle ever spots her wandering, it attacks and destroys her at once.

One of the amphibious birds is the theokronos, believed to be a bastard offspring of eagles and hawks. This is the old story told of its birth: there is a kind of hawk so lustful that, in the spring season, it lays aside all its strength, and is even bitten by the smallest sparrows; but when summer comes, and the air burns with the Dog Star's heat, it takes back its power, and frightens the sparrows with its shrieking, and seizes and eats them, seeming somehow to be calling in the insults done to it before. But if it should hear a female eagle, it flies to her and mates with her repeatedly, deceiving her; and she, made pregnant by the inferior bird, does not deign to warm the eggs that are born, and flies far from the male eagles, so as not to be discovered; for, if they perceived it, they would surely destroy her, driving her out for her adultery. And when the eggs are warmed by the sun's rays, the chicks that hatch are deadly to the amphibious fish.

There is also a bird called the 'gyges,' which is always crying out, and seems to think it is singing, and takes its name from this, and which devours the amphibious birds by night. If someone cuts out its tongue with bronze and gives it to a child who does not yet speak, it will certainly loosen the child's silence quickly.

Most wise are the counsels of the loudest-crying cranes, and this too must be known about them: when they are about to leave Thrace, once all have gathered together, one purifies the rest, and cries out, and so they all fly off together, that one alone remaining which purified them once assembled; and they place the older ones first in the flight, so that they are not forced to struggle to keep up with the younger ones. They cry out so as not to be separated from one another, and if they perceive that one is tired, two take hold of the weary one on either side with their wings and lighten her, or even carry her upon their backs, easing the labor of the journey; and they fly in formation, as of men marshaled for war, and at other times, once gathered, they stretch out again lengthwise, carrying stones in their feet, which, once dropped, let them know whether their flight is passing over land or over sea. They rejoice in fair weather; but if they perceive a storm coming, they put in to land until calm weather returns steadily, and when night overtakes them, they hurry to rivers, and settle amid the hillocks there, which the water, splitting around them, flows past like islands. And they do this from fear of beasts that would lie in wait for them, since these are either unable to cross the water, or, in doing so, make some sound that would rouse the cranes and put them entirely to flight. They sleep standing on one leg, and cover their heads with their wings. Certain ones go about as their guards and leaders, and if they perceive a man or a beast approaching, they cry out loudly and signal the attack, so that the rest may escape in time.

Geese too, likewise, have leaders in their flight and guards, always crying out, for their sleep; for, using a most unpleasant voice, they very rarely keep silent, so much so that they put stones in their mouths, when silence is needed, since they cannot restrain it otherwise; and they do this out of fear of eagles, whenever they must fly over the Taurus mountain range. In this they are most intelligent, but foolish about their pastures: for they very easily forget places, even if they find the finest pasture there, and for this reason are always wandering; and there is even some profit for them in such wandering, for they are not easily caught by those accustomed to watch the haunts of birds and scatter seeds there for that purpose, since, through forgetfulness, they do not come to the same places again.

Swans feed in the meadows, and on the shores, and by the lakes, and the crags and ravines echo back their song, and we know these to be the most musical of all birds, and we call them sacred to Apollo. They sing not mournfully, as the halcyons do, but sweetly and honey-toned, as though playing flutes or lyres. They are also very strong, and, flying often to great heights, fight against eagles, whether the eagles attack them or their chicks; yet they do not begin the fight, but love peace, for as long as they are allowed to sing, since they consider this sweeter even than food. They sing even before the sun rises, since then, in solitude, their cries are heard more clearly, and on the shores of the open sea, unless there is a storm, and the crash of the waves keeps them from singing, since they would not be heard even by their own songs. And they will remember their song, even if old age brings them to their end; though it grows weaker than in their youth, since they can no longer stretch out their neck or spread their wings, they use the west wind to help their melody, their legs now sluggish and their limbs weaker. And the one about to die withdraws to some place where no other bird will hear it singing, and no other swan disturbs the one that sings, knowing that the same end will befall itself too, if it happens to be nearby.

Hearing what follows, mightiest king, you will know that men are bold not only against the land and the sea, but now even reach out toward the very air itself, attempting the far-wandering birds. For hunters and fishermen, indeed, fear often meets them more than delight, whether one considers the winds that shatter their boats on the open sea, or the strength of sea-monsters, by which they are very swiftly destroyed, or the lairs of wild beasts in the mountains, from which the beasts often attack hunters unseen beforehand, so that they can neither hold their ground nor escape — indeed, warring against beasts, they are often struck down and destroyed, and fall to their ruin from cliffs in rough terrain. But for fowlers there is no such danger from birds, or from this kind of hunt, since they need not go, of necessity, to the ridges of the mountains, nor to the ravines; for it suffices them to wander delightedly over the plains, and the groves, and the meadows, and to hear the sweet voice of singing birds, using neither swords, nor clubs, nor spears, nor bringing nets and dogs with them, but birdlime and reeds, by which their path of hunting leads into the air, and fine nets and creels, very light to carry under the arm; and sometimes too a plant, around which they have placed borrowed branches, and they also bring along tame birds to share in the catch. It is fitting that fowlers be swift, and skillful with their hands, and sharp-sighted, and gifted by nature for schemes [...], so that, if need be, they can even imitate the cry of birds, so that, seeing them leaping about among the tree-trunks, the birds may follow. One must, then, divide the work of the hunt according to need, using birdlime, or horsehair, or nets, or snares, or even folding traps, or luring with food, or showing a bird of the same kind.

With birdlime are caught larks, and the swift goldfinches, and the lightest of all, the ampelions, and the weak buntings, and the baritai, and the sodes, and finches, and turtledoves, and the 'stars,' which have a red circle, like a star, upon their head. These, together with the other small birds that come in flocks from the north, are hunted with birdlime, once they have perched on the reeds.

Certain other small birds are also caught in their thicket by the following device: men bind together two branches of myrtle, bending them down at the bottom, and, tying a noose from a thin cord to one, run the cord through the other branch and fasten it tight with a small, firm peg; this serves as a perch for the little birds, and, if they settle there wanting to sleep, the peg easily slips from the hole in the branch, and the noose, spinning round, catches fast around the little bird's feet.

Finches and turtledoves are hunted under a tree, if they see a bird of their own kind perched on the tree's branches. But this method of hunting is not always to be used, only in snowy and wintry weather, once the plants are already bare and have shed their leaves; for then the little birds, needing a perch and shelter, fly toward these false, contrived branches as though they were real. It is a most pleasant sight to see little birds bound fast by birdlime, falling down.

And this too is most charming: if a hawk is brought along and set down near the trunk of a plant, the little birds, terrified, try to hide unnoticed beneath the leaves, glancing sideways at the hawk, bound fast by their fear, like travelers in anguish at the sudden sight of a robber, who, even after the terrifying sight has passed, dare neither run back nor go forward — so great a fear grips the little birds too as they gaze at the hawk. And the hunter, taking advantage of the fear thus displayed, at his leisure pulls them, utterly terrified, down from the tree.
Some birds, too, wanting sleep in the thick fields, fall into woven nets, when night comes on after sunset.

Partridges are caught with nets and folding traps, or by the sound of a partridge, or provoked to fight, or by the hide of a stag; for, loving this animal extraordinarily, they are deceived, if a man, putting on a stag's hide and placing horns on his forehead, approaches them unnoticed, and, thinking it truly a stag, they attend to it, and rejoice as it draws near, and are unwilling even to leave its side, as though watching some familiar companion of their own age after a long absence. But the fruit of their love is to fall into snares, or into nets fitted with dense lead weights, and then, instead of a stag, to see the hunter and the deception.

The same love that partridges have for stags, bustards have for horses, and from this a certain method has been devised against them: setting up nets near a river or a lake in a suitable spot, and leaving a small passage between them, wide enough for a single rider to pass through, a man shows the bustards a horse; and they follow it eagerly, spreading all their feathers, until the rider runs through that narrow passage, and all the bustards become entangled in the nets.

Quails are hunted by night in cloudy weather by means of older quails crying out; for the birds, rushing toward the sound, fall into the nets. There is also a certain method of catching them by day: a man spreads a net on the ground, and, raising his own cloak above his head and holding it up on either side with reeds, moves it, advancing little by little; and fear comes over the quails at the shadow of the garment nodding this way and that, until, fleeing it, they fall into the meshes of the nets.
Francolins too may be caught in this manner: since they trust more in the speed of their feet than in flight, the hunter, bringing dogs, will hunt them as he would hares.

Cranes are caught by other methods: if one cuts the neck from a dry gourd, and, hollowing it out, smears the inside with birdlime and puts a beetle inside; the beetle, wanting to make its way out, will make a noise, and, running up at the sound, the crane will lower its head, and, catching the beetle, will also drag along the hollow of the gourd itself, which sticks around its forehead and eyes, and glues itself to its feathers, so that it can neither see nor go forward, but stays still and stands, until the hunter, approaching, seizes it with his hands. And if there is no beetle available, it suffices to put an onion leaf into the hollow of the gourd instead. Cranes are also easily caught with traps, if one cuts a reed and, boring holes at its two ends, inserts thin twigs, making a double fork on them, through which he will run the noose round, hanging a pierced stone below, and, in the middle of the reed, inserting a thin iron pin and fixing a bean to it, at which the crane, looking, thrusts its head into the noose, and seizes the bean, but, wishing to draw back its head, pulls the noose tight around its neck; then, perceiving the trick, it will try many times to fly up, but will be dragged down by the weight of the stone, until the hunter takes hold of it.

Wood-pigeons are most difficult to catch by any device; for, perceiving hunters very quickly, they flee at once; yet they too are overcome by trickery: for the hunter, seeing them perched on a tree, spreads a fine net over the ground, scattering chaff over it so as to hide it, and sets up other wood-pigeons, taken previously, which he has blinded and bound their feet with thin cords, by which, moving them, he forces them to flutter about. Hearing the noise, the rest run up, abandoning their pasture and the trees; then the hunter, hidden beneath some hut, draws tight, with great strength, the cord of the nets, and, raising all the stakes together, catches the wood-pigeons that have fallen into the folds of the net. Doves too are caught by such decoys, but one might hunt them still more easily with a simple snare.

Blackbirds, and the sweet-voiced nightingales, may be caught by setting a trap in dense thickets, which has two circular rims, hidden beneath the twisted folds of the net and resembling fish-traps of the sea; ox-sinews are stretched taut, with a very long rod lying in the middle; from it they hang a cord and a trigger-cord, and they also place some bait, such as an earthworm from sand or earth, which, once the bird is lured by it, touches the trap and is caught fast, as those parts turn round, whatever has been arranged for the hunt. Against the blackbird, too, boys have devised something of this kind: around the time of winter, when the bird is most in want of food, they dig a pit and throw in an olive stone or a laurel berry, and set beside it a small piece of pottery; then upon it they place a peg looking into the pit, and against the peg they prop another shard of pottery, and stretch two twigs over the pit, on which a trigger-cord and another shell will rest. The blackbird, craving food, will surely draw near, and, once the shell suddenly falls, will be shut into the pit. In this same way thrushes and redwings too are caught.

The siskin is hunted with a cage, in which another, previously caught, is shut up to cry out, the cage having two doors on either side; the bait is a nut, or a grub, or something of the sort, toward which the bird, drawn by the voice, will rush. But a trigger-cord also spins these doors round, so that the siskin, once it has entered, can no longer fly out.

One could not easily catch the plover, unless one sets the net near water; for, needing to drink, it flies to it, while the hunter, hidden meanwhile in a hut, and, tightening the net with a cord, will cover the plover as it drinks.

Turtledoves too are hunted, thirst leading them to a spring, near which the hunter sets up a reed with feathers tied to its tip, whose movement frightens them and drives them far off; but he sets down nearby another turtledove, one caught before, which, when they see it, they fly toward and settle around; and so, the net being drawn up, they are caught.

Larks are caught by means of an owl, which the hunter, setting it upon a bronze hoop, shakes, continually pulling taut cords and placing round it, in a circle, little rods smeared beforehand with birdlime. For the larks, hastening to catch the owl [the night bird], are caught by the birdlime and the rods.

For the shrill-voiced jackdaws such a hunt is prepared: one must fix a long rod in the ground, and attach to it a noose of cord, with a trigger in the middle, covering the withies on either side as it turns; at its tip, right in line with the stretched noose, will lie an olive-fruit, and, if the jackdaws touch it, the trigger slips down, and the rod, coiled up, springs upright, and so draws the noose tight, so that the jackdaws' necks are caught as though by those of the hanged. And fowlers catch jays in the same way too.

There is another method of hunting jackdaws: a man fills a vessel with oil and sets it down, so that the jackdaws can see into it; and they, seeing their own shapes in the vessel, think them other jackdaws, and, flying down to the oil, leap in at once; then their feathers and all their limbs are weighed down, soaked in the oil, so that they cannot fly away, and so they are caught at once by this method.

If anyone wishes to catch a titmouse, he smears a goat's udder all over with birdlime; and the bird, hastening to drink the goat's milk, flies over the fence, and, coming to the pen, presses its beak against the goat's teat, and, the birdlime spreading as far as its claws, is caught.

For the hunting of the purple-coot one needs neither birdlime nor nets, but only to watch it as it sits somewhere alone, and, dancing, draw near little by little; for the sight of the dance is so pleasing to it that it will not fly away, even seeing the man approach, but will itself move its own limbs, dancing too, until it is caught, falling into the hands of the one who took up the dance for the sake of the hunt. And scops owls too are caught by hunters who dance and mock them.

Sea-birds are caught with hooks, on which little fish are set; and also, painting images of fish on boards, men hunt the plungers with them; for these, swooping down eagerly as though upon a fish, smash themselves against the boards and are destroyed. And others, not a few, are caught, as they swim, with snares, and nets, and traps, or even as they come to rest on certain headlands, where birds are accustomed to dry their feathers, or sleep, or rest after feeding.

With traps and snares, ducks are hunted, and net-weavers, and millet-birds, and other kinds of geese, and the swift phellinai, and coots, and very many other amphibious birds, deceived by food; for men scatter barley, or spelt, or millet along the edges of lakes or rivers.

Against geese, another device too has been contrived: a man makes a wooden goose, and, tying it with a rope, lets it go alone on the lake, and the geese gather round it and strike it, chasing it off as a stranger to their own flock; and the hunter, hidden in a hut and holding a thin cord, draws the wooden goose toward the land; and they, thinking it is fleeing, follow it, chasing it even within the nets; then the hunter, drawing up the poles and raising the net, covers all the geese together as they swim around the wooden one.

Nor do the birds called thraikes, nor the dytinoi and the divers, escape hunters, even if they swim the whole day through, but these too are caught by trickery. When the sea is unmoving from a calm, men board an oarless skiff and sail for a little way, so that the noise of the rowing does not drive the birds off; then one man stands at the stern, bringing a net, while another at the prow, gradually advancing the boat with the steering-oar, carries a lamp in a piece of pottery, which he shows, as it were, when he draws near the birds; and they, thinking they see not a lamp but a star, welcome the approaching boat, and, once it is near, the hunter hides the light in the hollow of the boat, so that the birds do not perceive the trick; then he casts the long net over them, spreading it out, and, covering many of them, draws it in. So much, then, mightiest king, can I say concerning the life and the hunting of birds; and Dionysius himself says that he was taught these things by Apollo, son of Leto.
